extracted.intended_audience: Korean central and local government regulators, policymakers, and regulatory reform practitioners (and OECD peer reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards on regulation, regulatory reform instruments, and governance arrangements in Korea (definitions, registry, RIA, stakeholder engagement, ex post evaluation, institutional oversight and related policies). Intended to inform design, implementation and assessment of regulatory policy in Korea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of regulation (Framework Act on Administrative Regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations refer to restrictions on the rights of citizens or duties imposed thereon by the central or local governments to accomplish a specific administrative objective, which are prescribed by Acts and subordinate statutes, municipal ordinances or municipal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Framework Act on Administrative Regulations clearly stipulates definition, objective and principles, as well as procedural requirements for the establishment, improvement, relaxation or abolishment of regulations. Specific details of regulations can be determined by presidential decrees, ordinances of the Prime Minister, and ordinances of the Central Administrative Agency, municipal ordinances or municipal rules, as entrusted by acts. No administrative agency can limit the rights of citizens or impose duties on citizens pursuant to regulations that are not stated in or delegated by the acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion from application (matters not covered by administrative regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affairs governed by the National Assembly, the Courts, the Constitutional Court, the Election Commission, and the Board of Audit and Inspection; affairs relevant to criminal matters, criminal administration, and security measures; matters relevant to information and security-related duties under the National Intelligence Service Act; matters relevant to enrolment, drafting, mobilisation and training under military service and defence-related Acts; matters relevant to military facilities, protection of military confidentiality, and defence industries; matters relevant to the items, rates, imposition and collection of taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are specified as exclusions from the application of the administrative regulation definition in the Framework Act; they delimit the scope of what is treated as administrative regulation for purposes of registry, RIA and other regulatory management tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of regulations (type, form, regulator, regulated party)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations were classified by regulator, regulated party and form. Type categories included economic (entry/price/transaction/quality), social, administrative; form examples included permission/authorisation/license/patent/approval/designation/recommendation/accession/test/examination/verification/identification/guidance/control/administrative penalty/reporting obligation/registration obligation/employment obligation/notification obligation/submission duty/standard setting, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulatory registry historically required indication of type and form; however, some regulations are cross-cutting and hard to classify. In 2015 the obligation to classify at registration was lifted and regulations are classified (responsible agency, themes, user description, life cycle) after registration to help the public find relevant regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory registry: registration by provision and system management
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2015 the regulatory registry system strictly requires all regulations to be registered by each regulatory provision without exception and links the system to the Ministry of Government Legislation’s National Law Information Centre for easy revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The registry has changed over time (1998 unit of administrative orders; 2007-08 consolidated units; 2009 push to register by provision). After the 2015 overhaul the government found fluctuating counts did not reflect actual size of regulations and that focusing on reducing counts did not equate to better quality; therefore the government stopped keeping track of the number of regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal bases and constitutional conformity of regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: All laws of Korea should be in accordance with the Constitution. Primary laws established by the National Assembly are the basis for all central and local government legislations (acts, presidential decrees, ordinances of the Prime Minister, ordinances of the Central Administrative Agency, municipal ordinances, and municipal rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations must be clearly stated in acts; details may be delegated via decrees and ordinances. The Framework Act provides procedural requirements for establishment, improvement, relaxation or abolishment of regulations, ensuring statutory delegation and constitutional conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Central administrative agencies are required to prove the legitimacy, necessity, and goodness-of-fit of each regulation they plan to introduce through RIA, and to conduct their own internal reviews prior to the final review of the Regulatory Reform Committee (RRC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA in Korea includes improving cost-benefit analysis; regulatory research centres (KDI, KIPA) support agencies with data analysis and capacity-building. RIA performance is measured in iREG across four categories (systematic adoption, methodology, transparency, oversight and quality control). RIA requirements apply to processes for developing primary laws initiated by the executive (survey focus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost‑in, Cost‑out (CICO) mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: CICO is a mechanism to restrict the increase of the costs of newly introduced or reinforced regulations by abolishing or relaxing regulations that carry an equal or more amount of costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CICO complements efforts to improve cost‑benefit analysis in RIA and establishes a way to continuously improve the quality of regulations. The Park administration adopted CICO replacing the former Regulatory Stock Management System.

rubrics_metrics.name: iREG composite indicators structure and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each composite indicator (for RIA, stakeholder engagement, ex post evaluation) is composed of four equally weighted categories: systematic adoption, methodology, transparency, and oversight and quality control. The maximum aggregate score is four (each category max one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While composite indicators integrate large amounts of information into an easily understood format, they cannot be context specific and cannot fully capture complex realities of quality, use and impact of regulatory policy. In‑depth OECD peer reviews are needed to complement the indicators. Results are sensitive to methodological choices and should not be interpreted as direct measurements of regulatory quality or used to assert relative performance among countries with similar scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement practices and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of online tools to improve information dissemination and participation, e.g., Regulatory Reform Sinmungo and the dedicated regulatory portal (http://better.go.kr), enabling citizens and businesses to access the portal and provide views and suggestions. Acceptance rate of the petition system increased by 36.6% in 2014 (4.6 times greater than previous year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: iREG measures stakeholder engagement for processes developing primary laws initiated by the executive. The 2014 Regulatory Indicators survey put stronger focus on evidence and examples to support country responses and on how different countries approach engagement requirements. Transparency and oversight are measured as part of the composite indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex post evaluation requirement and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Korea has formally required periodic ex post evaluation for all major primary laws and subordinate regulations developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex post evaluation permits identification of inconsistencies or overlaps and assessment of achievement of policy goals. However, as of the report there is no existing systematic or standard technique to support evaluations. iREG assesses ex post evaluation across the same four composite categories (methodology, transparency, systematic adoption, oversight and quality control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunset clauses and review mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of sunset clauses including outright sunset clauses (since 1998) and an extended 'review and sunset clause' (introduced 2009) requiring regular examination and verification of the necessity of existing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms are designed to secure better regulatory quality by requiring periodic review of regulations; combined with stock management systems they aim to prevent accumulation of unnecessary or obsolete regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary Regulatory Relief (TRR)
rubrics_metrics.description: TRR is a policy to temporarily suspend existing regulations on the private sector (introduced early 2009) designed to address economic challenges caused by crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRR represents an innovative regulatory policy tool allowing temporary deregulation to respond to economic shocks; it was used during the global financial tensions around 2008-09.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory oversight and institutional arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulatory Reform Committee (RRC) was mandated to review regulations to be newly introduced or reinforced, improve the quality of existing regulations, and manage the regulatory registry. Other institutional arrangements used across administrations include Public‑Private Joint Regulatory Reform Planning Initiative, Public‑Private Joint Regulation Advancement Initiative, Presidential Council on National Competitiveness (PCNC), the Regulation Information System (RIS), and Ministerial Meetings on Regulatory Reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight bodies and multi‑stakeholder initiatives are used to institutionalise reform, mobilise political leadership (e.g., President presiding or chairing meetings), and incorporate private sector input. Public broadcasting of Ministerial Meetings and public consultation channels (e.g., Sinmungo, RIS) are used to increase transparency and stakeholder participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance gap: legislative initiation and regulatory review
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislations initiated by the National Assembly are not subject to compulsory regulatory review vis-à-vis regulations initiated by the executive government; in 2015 about 94% of legislations proposed came from parliamentary initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hybrid constitutional arrangement weakens efforts to improve regulatory quality because good regulatory practices initiated by the executive may not apply to parliamentary initiatives. The share of primary laws initiated by the executive is low in Korea (16% over 2011-13), which creates a policy implementation and oversight gap that should be taken into consideration in regulatory governance reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles and objectives of regulatory policy (Park administration two‑track approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'two track' approach: reinforce regulations related to public safety and health while abolishing regulatory constraints that hinder economic vitality; regulatory reform as a tool to increase investment without additional fiscal burdens and to revitalise the economy and create jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Park administration reported KRW 5.7 trillion in economic impacts from improvements in 2015 (KRW 4.5 trillion induced investments and KRW 860 billion reduced regulatory costs). This principle guides prioritisation of reforms balancing protection and economic dynamism.
